parts.label: (a)
key_concepts: moving matter particles have wave nature
hints: Hint 1: Think beyond light - de Broglie suggested that matter in motion, like electrons, also has a wave-like property. What type of quantity would describe that wave?
parts.proper_answer: The wavelength associated with a moving particle.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Remember wave-particle duality**
You already know light can behave as a wave and as a particle. De Broglie turned this around and said matter particles like electrons, protons and even atoms also have a wave nature when they are moving.

Step 2: **Link to momentum**
That wave nature is described by $$\lambda = \frac{h}{p}$$ where $h$ is the Planck constant and $p$ is the momentum of the particle. So for 1 mark you just need to say it is the wavelength associated with a moving particle.

parts.label: (b)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Look at Fig. 7.2 - a central spot plus a bright ring. If electrons were just tiny bullets travelling straight, you would see only one small spot. What wave phenomenon spreads a beam into rings and bright and dark regions?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Read the pattern**
Fig. 7.2 shows a central bright spot with a concentric bright ring around it on the fluorescent screen. That is not what you expect from particles travelling in straight lines through a narrow hole.

Step 2: **Name the wave effect**
Spreading out through gaps of atomic size in the graphite crystal and forming rings is diffraction. So the phenomenon demonstrated is (electron) diffraction.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
key_concepts: diffraction and interference as wave-only behaviour
hints: Hint 1: Focus on what the screen shows - the beam has spread out and formed light and dark regions rather than a single dot. Which family of behaviours, particle or wave, can produce spreading and bright-dark fringes?
Hint 2: Connect that observation to electrons themselves - if only waves diffract and interfere, what must be true about the electron beam passing through graphite?
parts.proper_answer: The beam spreads out showing diffraction / bright and dark regions show interference. Diffraction and interference are wave behaviours, so electrons behave as waves.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Describe the evidence**
The electrons do not all land in one place. They spread out and form a central spot plus rings. That means bright regions where many electrons arrive and dark regions where few arrive - an interference pattern formed after diffraction by the atomic layers.

Step 2: **Draw the conclusion about nature**
Diffraction and interference can only be explained by waves. Particles on their own cannot cancel out to give dark fringes. Since the electron beam shows these effects, electrons must be behaving as waves in this experiment. This is direct evidence for wave-particle duality.

parts.label: (c)(i)
key_concepts: effect of accelerating p.d. on pattern scale
ring spacing decreases with higher energy
hints: Hint 1: The shape of the pattern does not change into something completely new - think what features were in Fig. 7.2 that must still be present in Fig. 7.3.

Hint 2: A larger accelerating p.d. will be shown in (c)(ii) to give a shorter de Broglie wavelength. For the same graphite spacing, what happens to the amount of spreading and the radius of the rings?
parts.proper_answer: Sketch shows a central spot with concentric ring(s), with the ring(s) of smaller diameter / closer together than in Fig. 7.2.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Keep the same type of pattern**
You still have electron diffraction, so you still draw a small central blob in the middle of the circle and one or more thin concentric rings around it, just like Fig. 7.2.

Step 2: **Make the pattern smaller**
With a greater p.d. the rings shrink inward. Draw the ring with a noticeably smaller radius than in Fig. 7.2, so the rings are closer together and closer to the centre. That shows less diffraction spreading.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
key_concepts: accelerating p.d. increases kinetic energy and momentum
shorter wavelength gives smaller diffraction angle
hints: Hint 1: Start with energy - a greater p.d. between cathode and anode does more work on each electron. What happens to the speed, kinetic energy and therefore momentum of the electrons?
Hint 2: Recall the de Broglie equation $\lambda = h/p$. If momentum $p$ increases, what happens to the wavelength $\lambda$?
Hint 3: Think of diffraction grating behaviour - for a fixed grating spacing, how does a smaller wavelength affect the diffraction angle and the spacing of rings on a distant screen?
parts.proper_answer: Greater p.d. gives electrons greater momentum. From $\lambda = h/p$, greater momentum gives smaller de Broglie wavelength. Smaller wavelength gives smaller diffraction angle / smaller angles for intensity maxima, so ring spacing decreases.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Greater p.d. means greater momentum**
The electric field does work $eV$ on each electron, so kinetic energy increases. Faster electrons have greater momentum $p = mv$. So increasing $V$ increases $p$.

Step 2: **Greater momentum means shorter wavelength**
De Broglie wavelength is $$\lambda = \frac{h}{p}$$ where $h$ is the Planck constant. Since $p$ is in the denominator, a larger $p$ gives a smaller $\lambda$. The electron wave gets shorter.

Step 3: **Shorter wavelength means less spreading**
For diffraction by the same graphite atomic spacing, a smaller $\lambda$ gives a smaller diffraction angle for each order, just as with light through a grating. The intensity maxima move closer to the centre, so the rings on the fluorescent screen are smaller and closer together.
